summary: Explains the reasoning behind the security design of Mobile IPv6 route optimization, which lets a mobile device and a peer talk directly instead of through a home agent. It records the thinking from 2001 to 2002 so implementers understand the design choices and designers of mobility or multihoming systems can avoid common security pitfalls.

eli5.summary: When someone moves house, mail can go through their old address or straight to the new one. This memo explains how to make the shortcut safe, so nobody can trick the post office into sending your letters to the wrong place.

questions: why is mobile ipv6 route optimization designed this way
what is mobile ipv6 route optimization
why does mobile ipv6 not use ipsec for route optimization
what attacks does mobile ipv6 route optimization allow
subtitle: Why Mobile IPv6 checks that a mobile node is really reachable at both its addresses before a peer will send it traffic directly.

tldr.problem: Route optimization lets a peer send packets straight to a mobile node's current address, but an attacker who could forge the required updates could steal traffic or flood a victim.
tldr.mechanism: Return routability sends test tokens to the claimed home address and care-of address, and the mobile node must combine both tokens to authenticate its Binding Update. The peer stays stateless until then and keeps bindings for only a few minutes.
tldr.outcome: The design aims to be roughly as secure as the non-mobile IPv4 Internet of the time. It is slightly weaker, mainly because of time-shifting attacks, which the short lifetimes limit.

facts.label: Return routability messages
facts.value: HoTI, CoTI, HoT, CoT, then BU

today: RFC 4225 is an Informational RFC (December 2005) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records design reasoning and does not define a protocol; the Mobile IPv6 specification it explains is RFC 3775.

sections.title: Purpose and Design Goals
sections.content:
RFC 4225 is an account of the rationale behind the Mobile IPv6 (MIPv6) route optimization security design, produced in 2001 to 2002. It is not a guide for implementors and does not present a new design. Its two audiences are implementors who want to understand the design choices, and people working on mobility or multihoming who want to avoid security pitfalls.

The design followed three principles. First, the end-to-end principle: mobility state is kept mainly at the home agent and, with route optimization, at the peers. Second, different trust assumptions: a mobile node and its home agent are assumed to know each other through a prior arrangement, but a mobile node and a correspondent node are assumed to have no prior arrangement at all. Third, a practical protection level: be "as secure as the (non-mobile) IPv4 Internet" was at the time.

The design also assumes that the routing infrastructure is secure and well functioning. If it is not, the memo says the Internet itself is broken.
sections.eli5: The goal was not a perfect lock, just one about as good as the locks the old Internet already had, and one that works between strangers.

sections.title: Route Optimization Basics
sections.content:
A mobile node (MN) has a stable home address and a temporary care-of address where it currently is. A home agent (HA) acts as a stationary proxy: it intercepts packets for the home address and tunnels them to the care-of address. That makes paths longer, which is sometimes called triangular routing.

With route optimization (RO), the mobile node sends its care-of address to a correspondent node (CN) in a Binding Update (BU). The correspondent stores the pair in its Binding Cache as a local routing exception, then sends packets straight to the care-of address with a type 2 routing header carrying the home address. That header type was chosen to avoid the risks of the more general type 0.

The danger lies in unauthorized creation of Binding Cache Entries. Without protection, an attacker could act from anywhere in the Internet instead of only from the path between two nodes, and could act well before the real attack. The memo calls these space shifting and time shifting. Because mobile and stationary addresses look the same, any IPv6 node may be a target, and a node in the correspondent role is the weakest.
sections.eli5: Normally your mail goes to your old home, which forwards it. A shortcut lets people mail you directly, but then a trickster could lie to the senders about where you live.

sections.title: Threats the Design Considered
sections.content:
The memo considers only active attackers and sorts threats into three groups.

  • Address stealing. A forged Binding Update could redirect packets to an attacker (hijacking, or man-in-the-middle when both peers are fooled), or to a nonexistent address (denial of service). Well-known servers such as DNS servers are the most vulnerable, so the design cannot rely on mobile nodes noticing a theft. A "future" stealing attack is limited by short binding lifetimes. Replay is limited by lifetime, nonces, a sequence number and a MAC.
  • Flooding. Redirecting a heavy stream, such as a video, to a victim's address, while the attacker spoofs acknowledgements. The memo says designers wrongly assumed the victim would send a TCP Reset; in practice it does not, so the attack is more effective than believed. Return-to-home flooding aims the stream at a home network instead.
  • Attacks on the Binding Update protocol itself. Spoofed packets can induce many unnecessary Binding Updates, fill a Binding Cache to force non-optimized routing, or use the protocol for reflection and amplification. Nodes can limit the resources spent on updates or turn route optimization off.

The memo also explains why plain IPsec was not used for arbitrary peers: it needs a global key infrastructure that does not exist. Even a secure reverse DNS would not verify the care-of address, so a return routability check would still be needed.
sections.eli5: A liar could say you moved to a spot where your mail gets lost, or point a flood of mail at an innocent house. The memo lists these tricks one by one and says how each is handled.

sections.title: Return Routability and Short Lifetimes
sections.content:
Return routability (RR) checks that a node answers at a claimed address. The mobile node sends a Home Test Init (HoTI) through the home agent and a Care-of Test Init (CoTI) directly. The correspondent replies to each with one packet to its source address: a Home Test (HoT) and a Care-of Test (CoT), each carrying a token. Two separate triggers are used so the correspondent never sends two packets in reply to one, which would allow amplification, and never replies to a different address, which would allow reflection.

Each token is a hash over a secret key known only to the correspondent (Kcn), the address and a nonce, with a final 0 for the home token and 1 for the care-of token so the two cannot be swapped. From both tokens the mobile node derives the binding key Kbm. The Binding Update carries the two nonce indices and a MAC keyed with Kbm, so the correspondent can re-create the tokens and verify the update. The home test travels from the home agent to the mobile node inside an IPsec ESP tunnel.

The correspondent can remain stateless until a valid Binding Update arrives, so the test messages cost no memory, and the mobile node is solely responsible for retransmissions. Token validity, and so binding lifetime, is limited to a few minutes. The memo admits the cost: a Home Test Init and Home Test exchange is needed every few minutes, and the home agent becomes a single point of failure.
sections.eli5: You send one secret code to the old address and one to the new address. Only someone who can read both can prove the move is real. The proof expires in a few minutes, so a trickster cannot keep using it.

sections.title: Residual Threats and Limits
sections.content:
The memo says the design was never meant to be fully secure and that the result is slightly less secure than IPv4, but the difference is small. The one significant difference it names is time shifting: a false binding keeps working until it expires. The short binding lifetimes restrict that. It also says new subtle problems will probably be found and that the design will likely need revising.

On IPsec, the base specification does not say how to use it between a mobile node and a correspondent. Where a relationship exists, it may be possible to create Kbm another way, but a care-of address check is still needed to defend against flooding.

Two further cases are covered. An attacker could pretend to be a neighbor by using a fake care-of address on the local link, but this is limited to neighbors and also hurts the attacker. When two mobile nodes talk to each other, the node acting as correspondent should tunnel its Home Test messages through its home agent so a co-located attacker cannot learn them.
sections.eli5: The lock is not perfect. A trickster who was in the right place once can sneak in for a few minutes afterward, and the design keeps that window small.
